newsitem.title: FRANCE: FIGURE SKATING-CANDELORO YEARNS TO BE BACK AMONG THE BEST.
newsitem.headline: FIGURE SKATING-CANDELORO YEARNS TO BE BACK AMONG THE BEST.

text.p: Philippe Candeloro does not consider himself one of "the big guys" in men's figure skating despite winning silver medals in past European and world championships.
But the popular Frenchman knows he could again be one of the best if he wins the battle against the skaters from the former Soviet Union for the European title on Thursday night.
Candeloro, 25 next month, is the only competitor in the top nine in Wednesday's short programme not from the old Soviet Union, which broke up in 1991.
He is lying fourth, among three skaters from Russia, three from Ukraine, one former Russian now skating for Azerbaijan and a former Latvian now representing Germany.
"I skate after them and if the big guys skate well, it will be hard for me. But if they make mistakes, I have a chance," Candeloro said.
"Then I can be a big guy again, too."
Ranged ahead of him are 1995 champion Ilya Kulik of Russia, titleholder Viacheslav Zagorodniuk of Ukraine and the surprising ex-Latvian, Andrei Vlaschenko of Germany.
Behind Candeloro are two more Russians, including Olympic champion Alexei Urmanov in sixth place, two more Ukrainians and the Azerbaijani Igor Pashkevitch.

Three years ago it seemed certain that Candeloro would stay in the thick of every title fight. He had been second in the 1993 Europeans, then took bronze in the Lillehammer Olympics in 1994 and silver in the world championships a month later.
Elvis Stojko of Canada narrowly beat him that time in what Candeloro felt was merely the first of several battles the pair would wage up to the 1998 Olympics.

It has not worked out that way. After a third place in the 1995 worlds, Candeloro sustained an ankle injury which plagued him through the 1996 season and he finished fifth in the Europeans and ninth in the world championships after destructive short programmes.

On Wednesday, he avoided serious error as he reached a contending position. "But I was afraid to start the short programme because when you live with something that bad, you always think about it, you never forget it," he said.

The troublesome ankle, on which he had surgery last May which kept him out of skating until November, still aches on the landing of certain jumps, yet he still achieved his first short programme triple-triple jump combination on Wednesday.

His free skating routine, based on the French military hero Napoleon, will include a similar combination and the usual array of jumps including the lutz, which caused him difficulty on Wednesday because of his ankle.
"But it is easier in the free skating because I can go into it more slowly," he said.
Whatever happens here, Candeloro is already looking forward to the world championships in Lausanne next month, the last before next year's Olympics in Nagano, Japan.
"It is a big world championship," he said. "There are seven or eight guys who can be on the podium. I want to be one of them."
